headline.statement: Table III prints video-only medical hold as 1.27% of n = 80, a share no integer count at that n can produce (1/80 is 1.25%; 1.27% is 1/79, the adjacent cell).
headline.evidence: Table III: Medical hold 1.27 | 1.27 | .99, under headers Video-only cohort (n = 80) and In-person cohort (n = 79). Results: 'There were no losses or exclusions of routinely collected and linked data.'
headline.plain: The paper says 1.27% of the 80 video-only trainees went on medical hold, but one person out of 80 is 1.25%, not 1.27%. That 1.27% is exactly one person in the other group of 79, and it is printed in the next cell.

findings.title: Video-only medical hold of 1.27% cannot be produced from the stated n of 80
findings.location: Table III, Medical hold row, video-only column
findings.reported: Medical hold 1.27% (video-only, n = 80) and 1.27% (in-person, n = 79), p = .99. The paper states there were no losses or exclusions of routinely collected and linked data.
findings.computed: R scrutiny (percentage share) rejects 1.27% at n = 80 and accepts it at n = 79; 1.25% at n = 80 is consistent (1/80). Pearson chi-squared on 1/80 vs 1/79 gives p = 0.992858, matching the printed .99. Stage-1 GRIM: implied count at n = 80 is 1.016; nearest attainable share is 1/80 = 1.25%.
findings.assumptions: The medical-hold percentage is a share of enrolled trainees. The paper's 'no losses or exclusions of routinely collected and linked data' makes n = 80 the analysis denominator for this row, not a survey-missingness problem.
findings.plain: The paper reports that 1.27% of 80 video-only trainees went on medical hold. One person out of 80 is 1.25%. 1.27% is one person out of 79 — the other group's size — and that same 1.27% sits in the next cell. The likeliest ordinary cause is that 1.27 was copied into both columns. The finding of no difference in medical hold is unchanged (one event in each group still gives p = .99).

passages.quote: There were no losses or exclusions of routinely collected and linked data.
passages.label: Results, after Table III

consequence.explanation: The printed p = .99 still matches one medical-hold event in each arm; only the video-only percentage is misstated, and training delays are not a load-bearing claim.

findings.reproduction_problem: THE COMMAND DISAGREES WITH THE FINDING: it reports `indeterminate` where the finding claims `impossible`. The command ran perfectly well -- that is the point. Re-read the finding before the paper.

findings.title: Survey percentages in Table III cannot be produced from the printed n of 80 and 79
findings.location: Table III, briefing-effectiveness and MVI-compliance survey rows; Methods completeness sentence
findings.reported: Column headers n = 80 and n = 79. Video-only: 95.89, 90.41, 14.86, 37.84, 20.27. In-person: 98.63, 34.25, 63.01, 8.22 (100% confidence is the remaining survey cell). Methods: 'all trainees completed questionnaires regarding their perceptions regarding the usefulness and effectiveness of their MVI briefing and were asked to quantify their MVI compliance.'
findings.computed: R scrutiny rejects those two-decimal shares at n = 80 and n = 79 and accepts them at n = 73 (video briefing items 95.89 and 90.41; all four in-person survey items) and n = 74 (video compliance 14.86, 37.84, 20.27). Stage-1 grim_sweep found no joint n ≤ 80 for the five video-only survey percentages. Pearson chi-squared on the reconstructed tables 70/73 vs 72/73, 66/73 vs 73/73, 11/74 vs 25/73, 28/74 vs 46/73, and 15/74 vs 6/73 reproduces the printed p-values .31, .007, .0063, .0023, and .037. Missingness versus enrolment is 6–7 people per arm.
findings.assumptions: The survey percentages are shares of respondents on each item. Item-level skip after a form was handed in remains possible; 'completed questionnaires' is not an explicit per-item completeness statement. The 6–7 person gap exceeds the three-patient-or-5%-of-n missingness bound used to separate ordinary available-case analysis from a reporting problem.
findings.plain: The paper says every trainee filled in the questionnaire and heads those rows with 80 and 79 people. The percentages only work if about 73 or 74 people answered, and the printed p-values match those smaller counts. About six or seven people's answers are missing from each group. The compliance comparisons still go in the same direction once that smaller sample is used; the table simply does not say that was the sample.

passages.quote: Furthermore, all trainees completed questionnaires regarding their perceptions regarding the usefulness and effectiveness of their MVI briefing and were asked to quantify their MVI compliance.
passages.label: Methods, data sources

passages.quote: | Found brief effective in explaining why MVI prescribed | 95.89                                        | 98.63                                        | .31                                          |
passages.label: Table III, Found brief effective

consequence.explanation: Printed survey p-values match Pearson chi-squared at the implied n of 73–74, so the significance claims survive; the column headers 80 and 79 are not the analysis denominators.

findings.reproduction_problem: THE COMMAND DISAGREES WITH THE FINDING: it reports `impossible` where the finding claims `suspicious`. The command ran perfectly well -- that is the point. Re-read the finding before the paper.

findings.title: Flights were randomized but injuries were tested as if trainees were independent
findings.location: Methods, randomization and analysis; Discussion limitations
findings.reported: Four flights were randomly assigned to two briefing modalities. 'Associations between categorical variables were analyzed using the chi-squared test.' Limitation (1): 'it used block rather than individual randomization.'
findings.computed: No intra-cluster correlation is printed, so a design effect cannot be recovered. Two clusters per arm is too few for a cluster-robust variance. Individual-level chi-squared on this design is anti-conservative for the injury tests that carry the title (p = .047 and p = .037).
findings.assumptions: This is a reviewer-supplied reporting and analysis standard (CONSORT 2010 cluster-trial extension, item 12a: how clustering was taken into account), not a standard the paper claims to follow. The authors already name block randomization as a limitation. Severity is capped at suspicious because the obligation is external.
findings.plain: Whole groups of about 40 trainees, not individual people, were assigned to the video or the in-person briefing, but the injury tests treated each trainee as an independent coin-flip. That makes a p-value of .047 look more decisive than the design supports. The authors list this as a limitation; they do not say how much it moves the result, and the paper does not contain the number needed to find out.

passages.quote: These  flights  were  randomly  assigned  to  cohorts,  which  would  receive  one  of  two  MVI-briefing  modalities.
passages.label: Methods, randomization

passages.quote: Associations between categorical variables were analyzed using the chi-squared test.
passages.label: Methods, statistical analysis

consequence.explanation: Ignoring clustering in a two-cluster-per-arm design anti-conservatively inflates the MSKI and BSI chi-squared tests that carry the paper's injury claims; the design effect is not recoverable from the printed numbers.

findings.title: Printed age means are too coarse to support the claim of no age difference
findings.location: Table II, Age row; Results sentence claiming no age difference
findings.reported: Age 21 ± 3 (video-only, n = 80) versus 23 ± 5 (in-person, n = 79). 'No significant differences in age or BMI between cohorts were detected.' No t, df, or p is printed for age.
findings.computed: Stage-1 uninformative-stat check on the 0-decimal means: attainable p-range [6e-07, 0.135], which straddles 0.05. Point Welch t from the rounded means is p = 0.002753 (Student p = 0.002581). Hedges' g from the same rounded statistics is −0.483, 95% CI [−0.801, −0.170]. BMI 24.1 ± 2.6 vs 24.0 ± 2.8 gives Welch p = 0.816, compatible with the NS claim.
findings.assumptions: The 0-decimal means and SDs are rounded as printed. The point p from those rounded values is not evidence the authors missed a significant difference: the paper's NS claim remains compatible with the rounding interval. This is the Heathers uninformative-statistics heuristic, a reviewer-supplied standard, so the finding is capped at suspicious. The flag-uninformative tool could not be re-run at this stage (denied); the p-range is the Stage-1 result, and the point t and effect size were re-run.
findings.plain: The paper says the two groups did not differ in age, but it only prints ages as 21 versus 23 years with no test. Numbers that coarse cannot show whether that claim is true. If the in-person group really was older, that could matter for injury comparisons; the printed figures do not settle it. Body-mass index, printed more finely, is compatible with no difference.

passages.quote: No significant differences in age or BMI between cohorts were detected.
passages.label: Results, paragraph 1

consequence.explanation: The 0-decimal age means are too coarse to confirm or refute the 'no significant difference in age' claim; a true age difference would be a confounder of the injury comparison.

findings.reported: Vitamin C (as ascorbic acid) 100 μg, 83% daily value for pregnant and lactating women. Adjacent Vitamin D is 10 μg (400 IU) at 67% DV; vitamins A, folate, and B12 also use μg.

report_markdown:
This study assigns four flights of female Air Force basic trainees (80 to a dietitian video, 79 to the same video plus an in-person briefing) and reports that the in-person briefing raised self-reported multivitamin compliance and cut musculoskeletal injury (31.25% vs 17.72%, p = .047) and bone-stress injury (15% vs 5.06%, p = .037).

Twenty-four of thirty-five numeric checks passed, including nine collapsed table-level passes. The injury percentages uniquely reconstruct as 25/80 versus 14/79 and 12/80 versus 4/79. Pearson chi-squared on those tables reproduces the printed p-values. The 43% and 66% relative risk reductions, the 7.4 number-needed-to-brief, and 5.4 injuries prevented per briefing of 40 all follow from the printed rates. Cohort sizes 80 + 79 = 159. BMI 24.1 ± 2.6 versus 24.0 ± 2.8 is compatible with no difference (Welch p = 0.816). Those are the numbers the title rests on, and they add up.

What does not add up is a training-delay cell in the same table. Medical hold is printed as 1.27% in both arms. One event in 79 trainees is 1.27%; one event in 80 is 1.25%. Both the Python GRIM engine and R scrutiny reject 1.27% at n = 80 and accept it at n = 79. The paper states there were no losses of routinely collected data, so 80 is the denominator that cell owed. The printed p = .99 still matches one event in each arm, so the non-difference claim is intact; the video-only percentage is the adjacent cell copied over.

The survey block of Table III is a different denominator problem. Methods says all trainees completed the questionnaires, and the columns are headed n = 80 and n = 79. Nine of ten two-decimal survey percentages are impossible at those ns. They are uniquely possible at 73 (briefing items) and 74 (compliance items) in the video-only arm and at 73 in the in-person arm — six or seven people short of enrolment. Pearson chi-squared on those reconstructed tables reproduces every printed survey p-value, so the tests used the smaller bases. Item-level skip after handing in a form is the ordinary reading; the completeness sentence is what makes the gap a reporting problem rather than a silent available-case convention.

Two further open questions, neither an arithmetic break in a printed figure. Allocation was by flight (two clusters per arm) and the analysis was an individual-level chi-squared; the authors list block randomization as a limitation, and that design makes p = .047 and p = .037 anti-conservative by an unknown factor. Age is printed as 21 ± 3 versus 23 ± 5 years with no t or p; the rounded point comparison would be a medium difference, but the 0-decimal rounding window for p straddles .05, so the claim of no age difference is uncheckable. Table I lists vitamin C as 100 μg at 83% daily value, which cannot be the same quantity as the milligram-scale pairing those facts conventionally describe.

Yates and Fisher on the injury tables would not meet α = 0.05; the paper named chi-squared and expected counts exceed 5, so Pearson is the test it ran. Uncorrected testing of ten Table III rows is ordinary; under that ten-test family three of six p < .05 results, including both injury tests, would be lost to Benjamini–Hochberg, while the two-test injury family loses none under that same rule.

The injury statistics reconcile with the tests printed beside them. The medical-hold percentage cannot be produced from its stated n, and the survey results were computed on a smaller sample than the table and Methods describe. Those two problems are not settled by the paper as printed.

questions_for_authors.question: Table III prints medical hold as 1.27% in the video-only column (n = 80) and 1.27% in the in-person column (n = 79). One of 79 is 1.27%; one of 80 is 1.25%. Could you send the medical-hold counts in each arm?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles whether the video-only 1.27% is a copy of the adjacent cell or a different denominator.

questions_for_authors.question: Table III survey percentages (for example 95.89% and 14.86% in the video-only column, 98.63% and 34.25% in the in-person column) do not match integer counts at the printed n of 80 and 79, but do match n = 73 and n = 74, and the printed p-values match chi-squared tests on those smaller bases. Methods says all trainees completed the questionnaires. Could you send the number of respondents for each survey item?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles whether the survey analysis used item-level available cases of 73–74 rather than the enrolment headers.

questions_for_authors.question: Table II reports age as 21 ± 3 versus 23 ± 5 years and the Results text says no significant age difference was detected, with no t or p printed. Could you send the unrounded means, SDs, and the test used for that comparison?
questions_for_authors.why: The 0-decimal means leave a p-range that straddles 0.05, so the NS age claim cannot be checked from the printed figures.

questions_for_authors.question: Table I lists Vitamin C as 100 μg at 83% daily value for pregnant and lactating women. Could you confirm whether the tablet contains 100 mg or 100 μg?
questions_for_authors.why: The printed unit is incompatible with the printed %DV given how μg is used on adjacent rows.

questions_for_authors.question: Age and BMI hypothesis tests: Would you be able to share the underlying values for this? Our reading of the article as published did not locate them, though they may well be somewhere we did not look, or in material we were not able to obtain. Summary statistics on their own would be enough.
questions_for_authors.why: Promoted from a check this review could not run. The review recorded: “Paper claims no significant differences but prints no t, df, or p. Recalculation from 0-decimal age means is uninformative (p-range straddles 0.05).” That is quoted rather than paraphrased, because the sentence is this review's reading and not a verified fact about the article -- if it is mistaken, the answer is simply that the values are where we did not look.
questions_for_authors.refusal_reason: Paper claims no significant differences but prints no t, df, or p. Recalculation from 0-decimal age means is uninformative (p-range straddles 0.05).

triage.reason: Same Table III survey-denominator problem as the grim_sweep finding; nine two-decimal cells fail at the header n and pass at 73–74.
Effect size from the rounded age means is the magnitude half of the uninformative-stat finding, not a separate defect.
The repeated clause 'a significantly higher proportion within the in-person cohort' is language residue, not a numeric defect.
Results prose 'most days (or more)' confirms the nested reading that removes the exclusive-sum-over-100% problem.
A summary-only paper whose data statement says the manuscript contains the relevant data is not a numeric contradiction.
The control-arm compliance rate is never printed, so the power statement is a reporting gap carried in not_checked, not an underpowered-versus-stated-parameters accusation.
Zero APA-form statistics is a fact about format; chi-squared was recalculated from reconstructed tables instead.
Uncorrected testing is ordinary; n_claims_lost_to_correction = 3 is arithmetic on a ten-test family the paper did not claim, recorded in the narrative rather than as an anomaly.
The load-bearing two-test injury family loses 0 claims under Benjamini–Hochberg; not an accusation.
